title: Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF)
summary: NETCONF is a protocol for installing, changing, and deleting the configuration of network devices. It uses XML for data and messages, and operations are remote procedure calls. This standards-track document replaces RFC 4741.

plainLanguage.summary: NETCONF is a protocol for changing the settings of routers and other network devices from a program. The program sends XML requests over an encrypted connection, and the device answers in XML. The protocol defines a small set of operations for reading and changing configuration data, plus optional extensions such as a draft copy of the configuration that is only applied when you commit it.

questions: how to configure network devices with xml
what is a netconf confirmed commit
subtitle: An XML-over-RPC protocol for reading, changing and safely committing the configuration of network devices.

tldr.problem: Network devices were configured through vendor-specific command lines, which are hard for programs to drive and hard to check for errors.
tldr.mechanism: NETCONF sends XML remote procedure calls over a secure, connection-oriented session. A small set of operations reads, edits, copies, locks and deletes configuration datastores, and optional capabilities add features such as a candidate datastore and confirmed commits.
tldr.outcome: It gives applications a formal interface that mirrors a device's native functions. RFC 6241 replaces RFC 4741 and has since been updated by RFC 7803 and RFC 8526.

today: RFC 6241 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4741. It has been updated by RFC 7803 and RFC 8526.

sections.title: What NETCONF Is For
sections.content:
NETCONF is a simple mechanism for managing a network device: configuration data can be retrieved, and new configuration data can be uploaded and manipulated. The device exposes a full, formal application programming interface (API), and applications use it to send and receive full or partial configuration data sets.

The protocol follows a remote procedure call (RPC) paradigm. A client encodes an RPC in XML and sends it to a server over a secure, connection-oriented session. The server answers with an XML reply. Both sides can check their messages against XML DTDs or schemas.

A key aim is that the management protocol should closely mirror the native functionality of the device. That lowers implementation cost and gives timely access to new features. The RFC also describes using XML transformation tools such as XSLT to turn a vendor-independent description of a desired network state into a form specific to one vendor, product and software release, and then sending that to the device with NETCONF.

Clients can discover which protocol extensions a server supports through a capabilities mechanism, and new capabilities, standard or proprietary, can be defined at any time.
sections.plainLanguage: NETCONF lets a program read and change the configuration of a network device. The program sends a request in XML over a secure connection. The device answers in XML. The protocol is designed so that its operations match what the device can do natively, which keeps it simple to implement and quick to pick up new features.

sections.title: Four Layers and Two Kinds of Data
sections.content:
NETCONF is conceptually split into four layers. Secure Transport carries the bytes; SSH, TLS and others are named as examples. Messages provides transport-independent framing with <rpc> and <rpc-reply>. Operations are the base protocol operations invoked as RPC methods. Content is the configuration or notification data itself, which this RFC leaves to separate data-modeling work; YANG, from RFC 6020, was developed to specify data models and operations.

The client is typically a script or application running as part of a network manager, and the server is typically the device. A device MUST support at least one NETCONF session and SHOULD support several. Global configuration changes made in one session are visible in all sessions.

The RFC also separates configuration data, the writable data needed to take a system from its default state to its current state, from state data, read-only status and statistics. Mixing them would make comparisons noisy, allow nonsensical writes to read-only items, make data sets large, and complicate restoring archives. So <get-config> returns configuration only, while <get> returns both.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol is described as four layers: a secure connection at the bottom, message framing above it, then the set of operations, and finally the configuration data itself. Settings you can change are kept separate from status values you can only read, so that a change request never tries to write a read-only value.

sections.title: RPC Messages and Errors
sections.content:
All messages MUST be well-formed XML encoded in UTF-8, and document type declarations MUST NOT appear. Protocol elements live in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:base:1.0.

A request is an <rpc> element with a mandatory message-id attribute chosen by the sender. The receiver does not interpret it and copies it into the matching <rpc-reply>. Any other attributes are returned unmodified too. The operation name is an element directly inside <rpc>, and its parameters sit inside that. A reply carries data, an <ok/> element when there is nothing to return, or one or more <rpc-error> elements.

Requests MUST be processed serially, but a client MAY send further requests before earlier ones finish, and responses MUST come back in request order.

An <rpc-error> can include error-type (transport, rpc, protocol or application, matching the four layers), error-tag, error-severity (error or warning), error-app-tag, error-path (an XPath), error-message and error-info. A server MUST NOT reveal application-level error information that the client lacks access rights to see.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request carries an identification string chosen by the sender, and the reply carries the same string back so that answers can be matched to requests. If something goes wrong, the reply describes the error with a type, a tag and a message. Requests are answered in the order they arrive.

sections.title: Datastores and Subtree Filtering
sections.content:
A configuration datastore is the complete set of configuration data needed to get a device from its initial default state into a desired operational state. It excludes state data and executive commands. The base model has only the <running> datastore, which always exists and holds the configuration currently active. Capabilities can add others, such as <candidate> and <startup>.

NETCONF itself does not define data models. It carries configuration inside a <config> element and treats the contents as opaque. Devices announce the data models they implement through capabilities, and a manager and a device may support several models, standard and proprietary.

Subtree filtering is the default way to select part of the data in <get> and <get-config>. A filter is a small XML tree built from five kinds of component: namespace selection, attribute match expressions, containment nodes, selection nodes (empty leaf elements) and content match nodes (leaf elements with simple text, matched exactly). Sibling content match nodes combine with AND. The RFC calls these filters useful but very limited, and notes that the server needs no data-model-specific logic to evaluate them. An empty filter selects nothing, which is not an error.
sections.plainLanguage: A datastore holds the full set of settings that define how the device should run. The running datastore always exists. Optional extensions add a draft datastore and a startup datastore. To read only part of a datastore, a client sends a small XML sample describing the pieces it wants; the device returns the matching parts.

sections.title: The Base Operations
sections.content:
The base protocol has nine operations. They retrieve, configure, copy and delete configuration datastores, and manage locks and sessions.

  • <get-config> retrieves all or part of a datastore, optionally narrowed by a <filter>.
  • <get> retrieves running configuration plus state data.
  • <edit-config> loads all or part of a configuration into a target datastore.
  • <copy-config> creates or replaces a whole datastore with another one.
  • <delete-config> deletes a datastore. The running datastore cannot be deleted.
  • <lock> and <unlock> take and release a lock on a datastore.
  • <close-session> ends a session gracefully, and <kill-session> forces another one to end.

An initiator SHOULD NOT assume an operation will succeed and SHOULD check every reply for errors.

In <edit-config>, an operation attribute on elements chooses what happens at that point: merge (the default), replace, create, delete or remove. The difference between the last two is that delete returns a data-missing error if the data is absent, while remove silently ignores it. The default-operation parameter can be merge, replace or none, and the error-option can be stop-on-error (the default), continue-on-error or rollback-on-error.
sections.plainLanguage: Nine operations cover the whole job: read a datastore, read everything including status, change part of a datastore, replace a whole datastore, delete one, lock and unlock, and end sessions. A change request marks each piece of new configuration with what to do: merge it, replace what is there, create it only if missing, or delete it.

sections.title: Capabilities and the Hello Exchange
sections.content:
A capability is functionality that supplements the base protocol, identified by a URI. Those defined here look like urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:{name}:1.x. The short form such as :candidate is for discussion only and MUST NOT be used inside the protocol. Anyone can define more capabilities, standard or proprietary, and a capability may depend on others.

When a session opens, each peer MUST immediately send a <hello> listing its capabilities, without waiting for the other side. Each MUST include the base capability urn:ietf:params:netconf:base:1.1, and the peers use the highest base version they share. If there is no common version, the session MUST NOT continue. Only the server's hello includes a <session-id>; a client that receives one, or a server that does not, MUST end the session.

The capabilities defined in this RFC are:

  • :writable-running allows writing directly to the running datastore.
  • :candidate adds a scratch datastore plus <commit> and <discard-changes>.
  • :confirmed-commit:1.1 adds a commit that reverts unless confirmed, and <cancel-commit>.
  • :rollback-on-error allows the rollback-on-error error option.
  • :validate:1.1 adds <validate> and the test-option parameter.
  • :startup adds a separate startup datastore, saved with an explicit <copy-config> from running.
  • :url lets a URL stand in for a source or target.
  • :xpath allows XPath expressions in filters.
sections.plainLanguage: At the start of every session, both sides immediately list the optional features they support. They agree on a protocol version, and the server tells the client the session number. Features are named by URI, and new ones can be added without changing the base protocol.

sections.title: Locks, Candidates and Confirmed Commits
sections.content:
A <lock> is meant to be short-lived. It lasts until released or until the session ends. A lock attempt MUST fail if any session or other entity, such as SNMP or a command-line script, already holds a lock on any part of the target, and the error then names the holder's session-id (0 if it is a non-NETCONF entity). <kill-session> can force-release another session's lock.

With the :candidate capability, a client edits a candidate copy and then issues <commit>. If the device cannot commit everything, running MUST stay unchanged. <discard-changes> reverts the candidate to the running configuration. Because the candidate can be shared between sessions, a client should lock it before modifying it; uncommitted changes are discarded when the lock is released.

A confirmed commit adds a safety net. Unless a confirming commit arrives within the timeout (600 seconds by default, adjustable with confirm-timeout), the device MUST revert to its prior configuration. The same revert happens if the issuing session ends or the device reboots, unless <persist> was given, in which case the confirming commit may come from any session by quoting a matching <persist-id>. <cancel-commit> reverts immediately without waiting for the timeout. For shared datastores, the RFC says locking SHOULD also be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Locks stop two programs from changing the same settings at once. The candidate capability lets you build a new configuration in a draft copy and apply it in one step. A confirmed commit applies the draft but rolls it back automatically unless you confirm it in time, so a mistake that cuts your connection does not leave the device misconfigured.

sections.title: Security and Transport
sections.content:
NETCONF depends on the transport for authentication, data integrity, confidentiality and replay protection. Connections MUST be authenticated, and the transport MUST provide a username to the other layers. An implementation MUST support the SSH mapping in RFC 6242.

The RFC does not define an authorization scheme, but implementors SHOULD provide a comprehensive one. Authorization of a NETCONF user may not map one-to-one to other interfaces, because data models can differ and the transport may offer its own mechanisms.

Configuration data is sensitive because it often holds passwords, user names, service descriptions and topology, so sending it unprotected invites eavesdropping and false data injection. Global operations MUST NOT let a user change data they are not authorised to change; for example, a user who may not set an interface address must not be able to commit a candidate that contains such a change made by someone else.

Unlocked changes can also have unintended results: a partly built access list could be committed from the candidate datastore, leaving a device insecure or unreachable. The RFC notes that <lock> shows NETCONF is meant for systems that trust their administrators at least somewhat, because a lock covers the whole datastore, even parts the holder might not otherwise access.
sections.plainLanguage: Device settings often contain secrets, so the connection must be encrypted and both sides must prove who they are. The protocol does not define who is allowed to change what; that is left to the implementation. The RFC also warns that changes should be locked while they are being prepared, so that a half-finished configuration cannot be applied by accident.
